pitchHistory.title: The Inference Wall: Why Scaling Laws Just Hit Their First Real Speed Bump
pitchHistory.summary: In late 2025, something quietly broke the AI industry's founding assumption: that more compute reliably buys you smarter models. The frontier labs are now burning billions on inference-time compute — chain-of-thought, test-time scaling, 'thinking' models — because pre-training returns are diminishing faster than anyone publicly admitted. This post unpacks what the engineering reality actually looks like, why it matters that we're shifting from a training-compute race to an inference-compute race, and what that means for who gets to build competitive AI systems in 2026 and beyond.

pitchHistory.title: Vibe Coding Is Real Now — and It's Going to Break Something Important
pitchHistory.summary: Andrej Karpathy coined 'vibe coding' barely a year ago as a half-joke, but in 2026 it's a genuine workflow: developers describe intent, AI writes the code, humans ship without fully reading what's underneath. This post digs into what that actually means for software quality, security, and the long-term craft of engineering — not with moral panic, but with a clear-eyed look at which risks are overblown and which ones should genuinely keep you up at night.

pitchHistory.title: The CPU Is Back. Blame the Agents.
pitchHistory.summary: For five years, every AI infrastructure conversation started and ended with GPUs. Now Nvidia — of all companies — is telling us the CPU has become the bottleneck, and it's betting billions on its own Vera CPU to fix it. This post digs into why agentic AI workloads are fundamentally different from training runs, why the GPU-centric stack wasn't designed for them, and what this quiet architectural shift means for the next generation of AI infrastructure.

pitchHistory.title: The Scanners Are Compromised: What the Trivy Attack Tells Us About Trusting Our Own Tools
pitchHistory.summary: On March 19, 2026, attackers poisoned Trivy — one of the most widely used open-source vulnerability scanners — turning the tool that was supposed to protect CI/CD pipelines into the weapon that raided them: 76 of 77 release tags retroactively repointed, credentials silently stolen, a self-propagating worm seeded across npm. The counterintuitive horror here isn't just another supply chain breach — it's that we handed attackers a master key by concentrating so much pipeline trust into security tooling itself. This post unpacks how the attack worked, why 'verify your dependencies' breaks down when your verifier is the thing that's compromised, and what a genuinely hardened build pipeline has to look like now.

pitchHistory.title: The License Is the Weapon: Why Google Just Fired a Shot Meta Didn't See Coming
pitchHistory.summary: Google just dropped Gemma 4 under a genuine Apache 2.0 license — making it the first frontier-class model from a major U.S. lab that's genuinely free to use, modify, and ship commercially without legal asterisks. That's not a product launch. That's a land grab. This post dissects why the licensing layer of AI has become the most important — and least understood — strategic battleground in tech, and why Meta's Llama 'open source' positioning is suddenly looking a lot shakier than it did last week.

pitchHistory.title: The Package That Poisoned 100 Million Downloads: What the Axios Attack Tells Us About the Lie at the Heart of npm
pitchHistory.summary: On March 31st, a North Korea-linked threat actor compromised a single maintainer account and silently backdoored two versions of axios — the JavaScript HTTP library sitting inside an estimated 100 million+ weekly download chains — before anyone noticed. This isn't just another supply chain horror story: it's evidence that the entire open-source package ecosystem is built on a trust model that was never designed to survive nation-state adversaries. The post uses the axios attack as a lens to examine why npm's identity and integrity guarantees are structurally broken, what 'trusted publishing' actually means, and why the hardest problem in developer security isn't the code you write — it's the code you didn't.

pitchHistory.title: TSMC Just Posted a 58% Profit Surge. That Should Terrify You.
pitchHistory.summary: TSMC's Q1 2026 earnings weren't just a record — they were a reminder that roughly 90% of the world's most advanced chips still come from a single island the size of Maryland. While everyone debates which AI model wins the benchmark wars, almost nobody is talking about the single point of failure underneath all of it: if Taiwan's fabs go dark, the entire AI boom ends on Tuesday. This post uses the earnings moment to trace the real supply chain fragility behind the AI gold rush — and asks whether $165 billion in Arizona really changes the math.

pitchHistory.title: The Junior Engineer Is Gone. Now What?
pitchHistory.summary: OpenAI just shipped GPT-5.3-Codex and GPT-5.5, both setting state-of-the-art benchmarks on real-world software engineering tasks — and the tech industry just cut nearly 80,000 jobs in Q1 2026, with almost half attributed to AI. The entry-level coding role that used to be how every engineer learned the craft is quietly disappearing, and nobody is talking seriously about what that actually breaks: the pipeline that produces senior engineers in the first place.

pitchHistory.title: The Phone Is the Next Typewriter: What the Qualcomm CEO Just Admitted Changes Everything
pitchHistory.summary: Qualcomm's CEO Cristiano Amon just revealed he's working with 'pretty much all' major AI players — including OpenAI and Meta — on secret next-generation devices designed to replace the smartphone as your primary computing surface. Meanwhile, leaked reports show OpenAI is co-developing a smartphone chip with Qualcomm and MediaTek, targeting 300–400 million annual shipments by 2028, with AI agents handling tasks instead of apps. This isn't a gadget story — it's about the deepest architectural shift in consumer computing since the iPhone, and the engineering decisions being made right now will determine who controls your digital life for the next two decades.

pitchHistory.title: The AI That's Too Dangerous to Release: What Anthropic Just Admitted by Building It Anyway
pitchHistory.summary: Anthropic built Claude Mythos Preview — by most benchmarks the most capable AI model ever constructed — and then refused to ship it publicly, locking it behind a $100M controlled-access consortium for defensive cybersecurity called Project Glasswing. This is the first time a frontier lab has openly acknowledged it built something it doesn't trust the world to have. The post digs into the engineering numbers, the logic (and contradictions) of building a weapon you won't sell, and what it means that the gap between what AI labs build privately and what the rest of us can touch just became a canyon.

pitchHistory.title: OpenAI Just Restructured Into a For-Profit. Here's the Engineering Decision Hidden Inside the Legal One.
pitchHistory.summary: OpenAI's conversion from a capped-profit to a full for-profit public benefit corporation isn't just a governance story — it's a systems architecture decision with irreversible consequences. When the entity that controls your safety research, your alignment teams, and your deployment guardrails is now directly answerable to shareholders and a $300B valuation, you've changed the incentive gradient at the root of the stack. This post argues that the real risk isn't that OpenAI 'goes evil' — it's that the organisational structure now systematically deprioritises the hard, slow, unsexy work that keeps powerful AI systems from failing in ways we won't notice until it's too late.

pitchHistory.title: Anthropic Built an AI That Writes 80% of Its Own Code. Then Filed for IPO. Then Asked Everyone to Panic.
pitchHistory.summary: On June 4th, Anthropic published receipts: Claude authored over 80% of production code merged in May 2026, up from low single digits sixteen months ago, with an 8× increase in shipping velocity. The same paper called for a US-China coordinated slowdown on frontier AI before recursive self-improvement becomes uncontrollable — one week after Anthropic confidentially filed for IPO. The cognitive dissonance is the story: this isn't abstract AI safety rhetoric, it's an engineering company simultaneously showing you how fast the car is going and admitting they're not sure the brakes work.

pitchHistory.title: Apple Just Shipped Google's AI Inside a Privacy-First Device. The Architecture Doesn't Add Up.
pitchHistory.summary: At WWDC26, Apple unveiled a rebuilt Siri co-developed with Google's Gemini, running on new on-device Foundation Models with a 'Private Cloud Compute' fallback — and declared it their AI turnaround. The features are fine. The real story is the engineering contradiction at the core: Apple is asking 1.5 billion users to trust that their most personal queries won't leave their device, while routing the hard ones to Google's servers. This post dissects the actual hardware-software-privacy tradeoff Apple made, why on-device inference at this scale is genuinely hard, and whether 'Private Cloud Compute' is a technical solution or a branding exercise.
pitchHistory.editorNotes: Word count is approximately 1450 words, slightly above the 1000-1400 target range (~7+ minute read).; The post references specific factual claims about a 'WWDC26' announcement — a future/hypothetical event. The Gemini fallback, the 3B parameter on-device model figure ('reportedly'), and the architecture details are presented largely as established fact. Since this concerns events that may not have occurred at time of writing, these claims should be sourced or more clearly qualified. The author does hedge with words like 'reportedly' and 'as Apple has described it' in places, which helps.; The '$160 billion in cash' figure is presented as fact without a cited source; recommend attribution.; Characterisations of Apple's and Google's business models and motives ('hoped users wouldn't look too closely') are opinion/inference — these are reasonably framed as analysis but could be more explicitly labelled as the author's interpretation.

pitchHistory.title: One Earnings Call Erased $1.4 Trillion. Here's What the Market Got Wrong About AI Chips.
pitchHistory.summary: When Broadcom's AI networking revenue missed analyst expectations by 14%, semiconductor stocks lost roughly $1.4 trillion in market cap in a single session — but the selloff wasn't really about Broadcom. It was the first visible crack between what chip companies promised and what hyperscalers actually need: the AI infrastructure thesis is hitting its first real stress test, and the most alarming signal wasn't the miss, it was the maintained outlook. This post unpacks the engineering and business model reality hiding inside the market panic — why the gap between GPU shipments and actual deployed inference capacity tells a more interesting story than any stock chart.

pitchHistory.title: Google Took 6,000 Pull Requests From Developers. Then It Closed the Door.
pitchHistory.summary: On June 18, Google cut off free API access to Gemini CLI — an 'open-source' terminal agent that had accumulated 100,000 GitHub stars and thousands of community contributions — and quietly pivoted to a closed enterprise replacement. This is the open-core bait-and-switch executed at scale: use community goodwill and free labour to build momentum, then monetise the exit. The deeper question isn't whether Google acted badly — it's whether 'open source' means anything when the model, the API, and the infrastructure are all proprietary from the start.
pitchHistory.editorNotes: Word count is approximately 1,450 words, slightly above the 1000–1400 target range (~7+ minutes read time). Minor trim recommended.; Several specific factual claims are stated without citation or qualification: '6,000 pull requests', '100,000 GitHub stars', and that Google 'closed the free API access' and 'pivoted to an enterprise product'. These are presented as established facts. Recommend linking to credible sources (e.g. the GitHub repo, Google's announcement) to substantiate the central premise.; The piece is clearly framed as opinion/commentary, which is appropriate. The author explicitly labels speculation about Google's motives ('The cynical read...', 'I don't think that's quite right') — this is well-handled. No change required, but ensure the factual backbone (the claims above) is verifiable since the opinion rests on it.; Characterisations of HashiCorp, Elastic, MongoDB open-core practices are general and reasonable but could benefit from light sourcing for accuracy.

pitchHistory.title: The Commerce Department Just Turned Off an AI Company's Best Models. Every Enterprise That Built on the API Noticed.
pitchHistory.summary: On June 12, the Bureau of Industry and Security ordered Anthropic to suspend access to its two most capable models for all foreign nationals — and because Anthropic couldn't reliably screen by nationality, it killed the models entirely, worldwide, overnight. It's the first time the 'supply chain risk' designation historically reserved for Huawei and ZTE has been applied to an American company. The real story isn't political: it's what happens to every business that built on a third-party AI API when a government can reach in and flip the switch.
pitchHistory.editorNotes: Word count is approximately 1500 words (~7.5 min read), slightly above the 5-7 minute target range.; Several factual claims about regulatory specifics (BIS authority over Huawei/ZTE, the AI diffusion rules proposed under Biden and modified under Trump, executive orders flagging foundation model weights, Google PaLM and OpenAI GPT-4 deprecations) are stated as fact without citations/links. These appear broadly accurate but would benefit from linked credible sources given the technical and legal specificity.; The opening scenario is clearly labelled as a hypothetical, which is good. The forward-looking risk assessment ('probability is not negligible') is appropriately qualified as opinion/speculation.

pitchHistory.title: Anthropic Just Published a 'Model Spec' That Tells Claude When to Disobey Its Operators. The Legal and Commercial Consequences Are Massive.
pitchHistory.summary: Anthropic quietly updated Claude's constitutional rules to include explicit conditions under which the model should override instructions from paying enterprise customers — not just extreme cases, but a broader category of 'operator overreach.' This isn't a safety blog post; it's a contractual and liability grenade thrown into the middle of every enterprise AI deployment. The post unpacks what the spec actually says, why it matters for anyone building on top of Claude's API, and whether Anthropic has just invented a new legal entity: an AI with enforceable duties of conscience.
pitchHistory.editorNotes: Word count is approximately 1400 words, at the upper edge of the target 5-7 minute range but within acceptable bounds.; The post makes numerous specific claims about the contents of Anthropic's Model Spec (quoted phrases like 'operator overreach,' 'principal hierarchy,' 'genuine care,' 'not unconditionally,' etc.). These are presented as direct quotations but no link, citation, or publication date to the actual Model Spec document is provided. Recommend adding a direct link/citation to the specific version of the Model Spec being quoted so readers can verify, and to protect against inaccuracy if the document has been updated or the quotes are paraphrased.; The legal analysis (fiduciary duty, product liability, 'legally naive thing to publish') is speculative commentary. It is mostly framed appropriately with hedging language ('if a court ever took that language seriously', 'may also be'), which is good. Ensure the piece continues to read as clearly-labelled opinion/analysis rather than settled legal fact — a brief explicit note that this is commentary and not legal advice would strengthen it, especially given point four recommends readers consult a lawyer.

pitchHistory.title: 88% of Companies Using AI Agents Got Breached. They're Deploying More Anyway.
pitchHistory.summary: A new industry report finds that nearly nine in ten organisations running AI agents experienced a security breach in the past year — and the response from the enterprise world has been to accelerate deployment, not pause it. This post digs into why AI agents are a categorically different attack surface than chatbots, what 'agentic breaches' actually look like in practice, and why the economics of competitive pressure are winning against basic security hygiene in a way we've seen before and should recognise.

pitchHistory.title: $850 Billion in Data Center Leases and the Grid Can't Keep Up. The AI Buildout Just Hit a Wall Made of Physics.
pitchHistory.summary: U.S. tech companies committed over $850 billion in data center leases in Q1 2026 alone — Meta added $79 billion in a single quarter — but the real constraint isn't chips or capital anymore. It's watts, water, and the 4-to-7 years it takes to get a new power substation permitted and built. This post examines what happens when the world's most capital-rich companies try to scale compute faster than physical infrastructure allows, why the bottleneck is now the electrical grid rather than silicon, and what that means for energy policy, smaller AI players, and the timeline of everything the labs are promising.
pitchHistory.editorNotes: Word count is approximately 1450 words, slightly above the 5-7 minute target range (~7.25 min read) — minor overshoot, acceptable but at the upper edge.; Several specific factual/numeric claims are stated without inline citation: '$850 billion' in data center investment, Meta's '$79 billion in a single quarter', FERC interconnection queue of 'over 2,700 gigawatts', US generation of '~4,200 TWh', and '~1,200 gigawatts' installed capacity. These figures are broadly plausible and align with widely reported estimates, but the piece would be stronger with linked sources. The Microsoft/Constellation (Three Mile Island) and Amazon nuclear co-location deals are accurately characterised as reported events.; The author appropriately qualifies speculation ('probably correctly', 'to be honest, unclear', 'Maybe.
